strengths: The proposed RSD framework is a sensible and well-motivated generalization of Denoising Score Distillation (DSD) from pure noise corruption to general corruption operators (blurring, inpainting, super-resolution, Fourier-domain subsampling), and the paper clearly situates itself within the Ambient Diffusion / Ambient Tweedie / DSD literature.

Empirical results are consistent and convincing on the core claim: the distilled one-step generator outperforms its teacher diffusion model across all tested tasks (CelebA-HQ 64x64 natural images and multi-coil FastMRI), with substantial FID gains (e.g., inpainting p=0.9: 25.53 -> 16.86; MRI R=4: 32.31 -> 10.71), plus a practical 25x inference speedup.

The paper introduces a practical contribution beyond the method itself: Proximal FID for model selection when clean data is unavailable, with quantitative evidence (Tab. 6) showing it tracks true FID reasonably well.

A theoretical analysis is provided showing that in a linear low-rank Gaussian setting, the distillation loss admits global minimizers aligned with the clean data eigenspace plus ker(A) perturbations, with an explicit Wasserstein-2 bound; the proof in Appendix D appears correct and complete.

Demonstrating direct distillation from publicly available pretrained checkpoints (Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-Space Ambient Diffusion) provides evidence of modularity and real-world applicability, including the extension to the complex-valued MRI domain.
Implementation details (Algorithm 6, Appendix G) are detailed enough to support reproducibility, and data-efficiency/early-training analysis (Fig. 5) addresses a natural concern about added cost.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core technical ingredient is applying the existing SiD/DSD distillation machinery to corruption-aware pretrained teachers, with the main algorithmic change being that generated samples are corrupted by A before training the fake diffusion model. This is a natural, incremental extension of DSD [6]; the paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is technically new beyond combining existing pieces (Appendix C only lists broad-brush differences).

Theoretical contribution is narrow: the analysis is restricted to a rank-1 (r=1), linear-Gaussian, perfectly-estimated-score setting and closely mirrors the DSD analysis; it does not explain the empirically observed teacher-beating behavior in realistic deep nonlinear regimes, so the claimed 'principled understanding' is somewhat overstated.

Evaluation scope is limited: experiments are confined to CelebA-HQ at 64x64 and one MRI dataset, with FID as essentially the sole quantitative metric. No higher-resolution results, no additional metrics (precision/recall, IS), and only one non-trivial external baseline (EM-Diffusion, which even uses 50 clean images). Comparisons to other unsupervised/semi-supervised approaches to learning from corrupted data are absent.

Several key results rely on publicly released teacher checkpoints rather than the authors' own Phase I training (random inpainting and MRI tasks), which weakens the evidence for the full integrated pipeline and the claimed unification across pretraining objectives.

Performance in the noisy Gaussian deblurring setting is notably weak (FID 76.98, worse than few-shot EM-Diffusion at 51.33), and the gap between best FID and proximal-FID-selected models is sizable in noisy regimes (e.g., 76.98 vs 88.29), suggesting the proposed model selection metric is less reliable exactly where it matters; this caveat is under-discussed.

The data-efficiency claim is somewhat misleading: distillation requires 50-100M image iterations (comparable to the ~100M used for pretraining), so the total training cost is high; the claim only refers to iterations needed to surpass the teacher, not overall efficiency.

No mention of code release, and the 'first distillation framework for general inverse problems' claim is strong given limited task coverage and the inability to perform conditional inference (acknowledged only in Appendix B).

strengths: The proposed framework is coherent and clearly presented: the two-phase structure (corruption-aware pretraining followed by one-step distillation) is easy to follow, and Algorithm 6 plus the appendix pseudocode make the method reproducible in outline.

Consistent empirical improvement over teacher diffusion models is observed across several corruption types (deblurring, inpainting, super-resolution, MRI acceleration), and the paper is commendably honest that it loses to EM-Diffusion on noisy Gaussian deblurring.

The ability to distill directly from publicly released Ambient Diffusion and Fourier-Space Ambient Diffusion checkpoints is a useful demonstration of modularity, and the MRI experiments extend the setting to the complex domain.
The proximal FID model-selection metric is a practical contribution for settings where clean data is unavailable, with an empirical check that it stays close to true FID (Table 6).
weaknesses: Limited novelty over the underlying components. The paper is essentially DSD [6] plus two modifications: (a) allowing a general corruption operator A in the pretraining and distillation losses, and (b) adopting SiD [52] as the distillation machinery. The pretraining objectives are taken verbatim from Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, and Fourier-Space Ambient Diffusion, and the distillation loss, alpha=1.2 setting, and proximal-FID model selection are all inherited from prior work. The genuinely new algorithmic content (corrupting generated samples by A before training the fake diffusion model, Lines 13/17 of Algorithm 6) is a small delta that is not analyzed or ablated in depth.

The theoretical contribution is thin and arguably mischaracterized. Theorem 1 is a rank-1, linear-Gaussian special case assuming a perfect score and a linear generator; the headline claim that RSD 'recovers the eigenspace of the clean data covariance matrix' is contradicted by the theorem itself, which shows the generator over-scales the true eigenvector by a noise-dependent factor sqrt(1 + sigma^2/||Ae||^2), i.e., a biased estimate, not recovery. The result is a modest generalization of the analysis already in DSD [6] (as the authors themselves acknowledge in Appendix C), and its relevance to the deep, nonlinear models used in the experiments is unclear.

Evaluation is narrow. All natural-image experiments are on CelebA-HQ at 64x64 resolution; no CIFAR, ImageNet, or higher-resolution results are provided. Only FID is reported; precision/recall, density/coverage, or any fidelity-diversity trade-off analysis is absent, which matters because distillation methods can trade diversity for FID. It remains open whether the method scales beyond toy-resolution faces.

The 'first distillation framework capable of addressing general inverse problems in an unsupervised setting' claim is overstated. The method learns an unconditional clean-data prior; it does not solve inverse problems (no conditional sampling given a measurement), as the authors concede in Appendix B. The comparison to EM-Diffusion is also somewhat apples-to-oranges since EM-Diffusion targets reconstruction-capable models.

Several headline results rely on distilling from publicly released checkpoints rather than the authors' own pretraining pipeline (Tables 3 and 4), so the end-to-end contribution is untested in those settings; the distillation stage alone, applied to third-party checkpoints, is the actual contribution there.

The 'data efficiency' claim (Sec. 5.4) is misleading: distillation requires 50-100 million image iterations, comparable to the ~100 million iterations needed for EDM pretraining. The method is not cheaper in compute than simply training the teacher; it is only cheaper than the teacher at inference.

Presentation and scholarship issues: references [8] and [9] are the identical Ambient Diffusion paper cited twice under different numbers; reference [1] lacks authors; there are typos ('Groudtruth' in Fig. 3, 'Muti-Coil MRI' in Appendix G.3); Fig. 2 lacks axis labels and task descriptions; and the discussion of why distillation improves upon the teacher (the paper's central empirical phenomenon) remains anecdotal, with the toy theory too weak to explain it.

FID under heavy corruption is fragile: for tasks like random inpainting p=0.9, FID of observations is ~400 and small FID differences among methods may not reflect perceptual quality; no user study or paired perceptual evaluation is provided.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framework: RSD extends DSD from pure-noise corruption (A = identity) to general corruption operators (blurring, masking, super-resolution, Fourier-domain subsampling), and cleanly decouples the pipeline into corruption-aware pretraining followed by one-step SiD-style distillation.

Consistent empirical gains over the teacher diffusion models across all evaluated tasks and noise regimes (Tables 2-4), including a practical multi-coil MRI application with complex-domain extension, demonstrating real-world relevance.

Good modularity: the framework is compatible with several existing corruption-aware pretraining objectives (Standard Diffusion, Ambient Tweedie, Ambient Diffusion, Fourier-Space Ambient Diffusion), and the authors demonstrate distilling directly from publicly released checkpoints, which strengthens reproducibility claims.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 1) provides a principled explanation of why distillation improves over the teacher: the distilled generator recovers the clean eigenspace up to a noise-dependent scaling, with a complete proof including Wasserstein-2 characterization in the linear regime.

Useful practical contributions beyond the main method: the proximal FID metric for unsupervised model selection (Sec. 5.3, Table 6), data-efficiency analysis of the distillation phase (Sec. 5.4), and inference speedup measurements (25x, Table 5).
Comparison to EM-Diffusion is favorable while using strictly less supervision (no clean images vs. 50-shot initialization), which strengthens the significance of the results.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty relative to DSD [6]: the core distillation machinery is essentially SiD [52] with corrupted generator outputs, and the main contribution is applying it with a general operator A. Appendix C itself confirms the contribution is largely an extension/generalization; the delta over DSD is real but incremental.

Evaluation scale is modest: all natural-image experiments are on CelebA-HQ at 64x64 resolution. There is no evidence on higher resolutions, CIFAR-10, ImageNet, or text-to-image settings, leaving generalization to modern-scale settings unverified.

The theory is quite restricted: rank-1 Gaussian data, linear corruption, linear generator, and perfect score estimation (Assumption 2). The gap between this analysis and the deep nonlinear setting used in experiments is large, so the theoretical 'eigenspace recovery' claim should be interpreted cautiously.

Results in the noisy Gaussian deblurring setting are notably weaker: RSD (76.98) is significantly worse than EM-Diffusion few-shot (51.33), and the noiseless deblurring FID (31.90) is also high relative to other tasks; the paper acknowledges but does not deeply analyze this failure mode.

Some baselines are reproduced rather than taken from original papers without error bars or variance estimates; FID on 50k samples for 64x64 CelebA is reported as single numbers, making the significance of small gaps (e.g., Table 3) hard to assess.

Proximal FID model selection can be substantially off in some settings (e.g., 88.29 selected vs. 76.98 best for noisy deblurring), which limits the reliability of the proposed unsupervised selection criterion, though this is disclosed honestly.

Several presentation issues: duplicate references ([8] and [9] are identical; [1] lacks authors), typos ('Groudtruth', 'auxilliary', 'Muti-Coil'), and some notational overload in the theory section that hurts readability.
Heavy reliance on publicly released teacher checkpoints from prior work for a substantial portion of the experiments (Tables 3 and 4), so the fully end-to-end pipeline is validated on fewer settings.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant problem: learning generative models from corrupted observations only, with a unified two-phase framework (corruption-aware diffusion pretraining followed by one-step score distillation) that gracefully handles diverse operators (identity, blur, masking, downsampling, Fourier undersampling) and both noisy and noiseless regimes.

Empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing: multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, FFHQ, CelebA-HQ, AFHQ-v2), multiple corruption tasks with parameter sweeps, a real-world multi-coil MRI case study, plus additional metrics (IS, Precision, Recall, KID), and ablations on data scale, noise misspecification, distillation losses, and heterogeneous noise levels.

Baselines are appropriate and current, including Ambient Diffusion, TweedieDiff, EM-Diffusion, SFBD, and clean-data upper bounds; the reported gains (e.g., RSD 4.77 vs Teacher-Truncated 12.21 on CIFAR-10 σ=0.2) are substantial and consistently favor the method.

The paper offers a genuinely interesting conceptual claim — that score distillation can improve sample quality in corrupted-data regimes, not merely accelerate sampling — supported by an intuitive mode-seeking/mode-covering argument and a substantial appendix with quantitative theoretical analysis (global minimizer characterization in linear Gaussian settings, strict saddle property, general Fisher-divergence guarantees under injectivity conditions).

Practical contributions beyond the core method: the Proximal FID model-selection criterion for corrupted-data training is a useful, well-validated addition, and the efficiency analysis (30x sampling speedup, distillation surpassing the teacher in ~4 hours vs 48 hours pretraining) is informative.

The method is modular: it can plug in different pretraining objectives and distillation losses, and the paper is transparent about limitations (e.g., that SDS/DMD underperformance may reflect default hyperparameters rather than intrinsic properties).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is limited: the core recipe is essentially (1) an existing corruption-aware diffusion objective for pretraining and (2) an existing distillation objective (SiD) applied to generator outputs passed through the corruption pipeline. The main contribution is the observation/combination rather than a new mechanism; the technical delta over SiD (Zhou et al., 2024) plus corruption-aware pretraining is relatively small.

The central claim that distillation improves quality under corruption may partly stem from known behavior of SiD (student outperforming teacher even on clean data) and from giving the student substantial additional training compute; the comparison to an equally compute-extended teacher is not fully addressed, so the marginal effect of the corruption-respecting distillation step specifically is somewhat under-isolated.

Theoretical results are confined to heavily stylized settings (perfect score estimation, low-rank linear Gaussian data, linear corruption), with conditions such as Poincaré-type inequalities and injectivity of the measurement operator that are difficult to verify for realistic settings; the theory provides intuition but not guarantees for the main experiments.

Some experimental details raise fairness questions: e.g., EM-Diffusion and Teacher Diffusion baselines for general corruptions appear weaker than expected (Teacher Diffusion worse than the blurred Observation in some rows), and the distillation-loss ablation shows DMD degrading sharply (7.48 vs SiD's 4.77) with defaults, making head-to-head claims sensitive to tuning choices.

Evaluation relies primarily on FID against the clean test distribution computed with access to clean data (for reporting); while Proximal FID is proposed for model selection, its general reliability across all operators (Table 11 gaps of 4–12 FID points) is not yet negligible.
FID computed on only 250 or 100 images for the inverse-problem evaluations (Table 9, Table 16) is a small sample size, limiting the statistical strength of those conclusions.

strengths: The paper is technically solid and well-organized. The two-phase framework (corruption-aware pretraining + SiD-style distillation) is clearly presented, and Algorithm 1 plus the appendix training procedures make the pipeline reproducible in principle.

The empirical coverage is broad and careful: denoising across CIFAR-10/FFHQ/CelebA-HQ/AFHQ-v2 and multiple noise levels, general operators (deblurring, inpainting, super-resolution) in both noiseless and noisy regimes, multi-coil MRI with several acceleration factors, ablations on data size, unknown sigma, misspecified sigma, and distillation losses.

The results that the one-step distilled student consistently beats its corrupted-data diffusion teacher are substantial (e.g., 12.21 -> 4.77 FID on CIFAR-10 denoising at sigma=0.2) and are supported by multiple metrics (IS, Precision, Recall, KID), not just FID.
Proximal FID is a practical and useful contribution: model selection without clean data is a real gap in this literature, and the tracking analysis (Tables 10-11, Figs. 5, 11, 12) is convincing.

The appendix theory (linear Gaussian low-rank analysis, rank-one landscape with strict saddle property, general Fisher-divergence bounds) is coherent and shows effort to explain the surprising improvement phenomenon.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The framework is essentially a composition of existing components: the pretraining objectives in Table 1 are all taken verbatim from prior work (Ambient Diffusion, TweedieDiff, Fourier-space ambient diffusion), and the distillation phase directly reuses SiD. The core claim that a distilled generator can outperform its teacher was already established (SiD, Zhou et al. 2024, explicitly reports teacher 2.39 -> student 1.55 on FFHQ). The contribution is applying a known phenomenon in a new regime, which is an empirical/incremental advance rather than a new method.

The 'corruption-respecting' distillation step (Algorithm 1, Line 6) is a fairly natural adaptation of the SiD loop; the paper does not isolate its necessity with an ablation showing what happens without corrupting generator outputs, which would be the key evidence that the adaptation matters.

The theory is far from the practice: it assumes perfect score estimation, linear/Gaussian low-rank data, and (for Theorem 2) a rank-one generator, none of which connect quantitatively to the FID gains observed. It reads as post-hoc rationalization rather than design guidance.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Table 2 supports 'surpasses all few-shot baselines' only for denoising; in Table 4, RSD loses to EM-Diffusion on Gaussian deblurring at sigma=0.2 (76.98 vs 51.33), and the abstract's blanket SOTA language does not acknowledge these cases.

Proximal FID selection leaves sizable gaps in the general-corruption tasks (e.g., 88.29 vs best 76.98; 27.42 vs 22.00 in Table 11), so headline numbers partly rely on oracle model selection, while the practical selection criterion is weaker than presented.

Presentation and reporting issues: the code URL in the abstract is empty; Table 4's bolding ('best results are highlighted') appears inconsistent; bracketed reference placeholders ([5], [34], [12]) are mixed with author-year citations; duplicated/erroneous references (Daras et al. 2023a listed twice with identical content; duplicate Diff-Instruct entries) suggest rushed preparation.

Experiments are confined to 64x64 images; there is no evidence the framework scales, and no comparison against a zero-shot variant of SFBD-style deconvolution or other iterative EM approaches that could also close the student-teacher gap.

The mode-seeking explanation (Sec. 4.9) is plausible but largely qualitative; the FID/Recall evidence is indirect and a cleaner empirical test of the 'distillation discards diffuse mass' hypothesis would strengthen the conceptual claim.

strengths: Strong and consistent empirical gains: RSD substantially improves FID over corruption-aware diffusion teachers across denoising (CIFAR-10 σ=0.2: 4.77 vs. teacher 12.21), general corruptions, and multi-coil MRI, and even approaches clean-data upper bounds (DDPM 3.21) despite training purely on corrupted data.

Practically important problem setting: learning generative models from corrupted-only observations is highly relevant for medical/scientific imaging, and the two-phase framework is modular—existing corruption-aware objectives (Ambient Diffusion, TweedieDiff, Fourier-space variants) plug into Phase I cleanly.

Comprehensive evaluation and ablations: multiple datasets, noise levels, missing rates, acceleration factors; ablations on distillation losses, data scale, unknown/misppecified σ, and heterogeneous noise; downstream conditional inverse problems demonstrate the learned prior's utility.

Useful practical contributions beyond the main method: the Proximal FID model-selection criterion addresses a real gap (how to select checkpoints without clean data) and is validated to track true FID closely; efficiency analysis (one-step generation, ~30× speedup, distillation surpassing teacher in ~4h) is well documented.

Substantial theoretical support in the appendix: closed-form global minimizers, Wasserstein-2 improvement bounds in linear Gaussian/low-rank settings, strict-saddle landscape analysis, multiple noise scales, and general Fisher-divergence guarantees, which lends credibility to the 'distillation beyond acceleration' claim.
Clear writing overall, with transparent discussion of limitations (e.g., acknowledging that SDS/DMD baselines used untuned defaults).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core recipe is essentially applying SiD distillation on top of existing corruption-aware diffusion teachers, plus applying the corruption pipeline to generator outputs during distillation. The 'unified framework' largely composes known components (Daras et al., Zhou et al.), and the genuinely new technical ingredient is thin.

Dependence on a single distillation loss: the ablation shows SDS diverges (>200 FID) and DMD substantially underperforms; only SiD works well with default hyperparameters. This raises concerns about the robustness and generality of the proposed distillation stage, and hyperparameters were not tuned for the baselines.

Theory is stylized and partially disconnected from the actual algorithm: the linear-Gaussian analysis assumes a perfect score estimate, a low-rank linear generator, and an idealized loss (real score in place of the fake score) rather than the SiD loss actually used; general guarantees rely on strong assumptions (Poincaré inequality, near-optimal fake score, injectivity).

Performance under noisy general corruptions is notably weaker: e.g., Gaussian deblurring at σ=0.2 yields FID 76.98, worse than the few-shot EM-Diffusion baseline (51.33), so the 'competitive with or exceeds few-shot methods' claim holds only selectively.

MRI comparison is limited: only teacher diffusion and an L1-EDM reconstruction baseline; no comparison to other published MRI generative priors, limiting the strength of the real-world applicability claim.

Minor presentation/reproducibility issues: the code URL in the abstract is blank; some results appear inconsistent across tables (e.g., inpainting best FID 16.79 in Table 11 vs. 16.86 in Table 4); Proximal FID against corrupted training data is heuristic and its theoretical justification (e.g., potential bias toward corruption-matching models) is not analyzed.
